post: We report a pre-registered [11C]UCB-J PET sub-study of a recently published randomized trial in which a single psilocybin dose produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in major depressive disorder (MDD).

Serotonergic psychedelics reliably alter affective tone, emotional regulation, and self-experience. Prevailing theories emphasize acute changes in neural entropy, default mode network integrity, and large-scale functional connectivity but do not offer a clear mechanism that explains how 5-HT2A receptor pharmacology relates to lasting changes in affect and self-related processing.

A recent publication by Xu et al. suggests that Gi activation following 5-HT2AR stimulation differentiates hallucinogenic from nonhallucinogenic agonists. Here, we reanalyze the author's source data to demonstrate that Gi activation is less predictive of hallucinogenic potential than canonical effectors of 5-HT2AR signaling.

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by dysfunction in higher-order cortical regions involved in emotional and cognitive processes; however, its neurobiological basis remains unclear. Pharmacological treatments, including esketamine and sertraline, produce rapid antidepressant effects.

The serotonin 5-HT 2A receptor (5-HT 2A R) signaling involves canonical G q/11 proteins and alternative pathways, such as recruitment of other G proteins. It has been proposed that the 5-HT 2A R-mediated activation of inhibitory G i/o proteins accounts for the hallucinogenic properties of psychedelics.

Ketamine exerts rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but its impact on working memory and neural circuitry remains unclear. This secondary analysis investigated behavioral and neural changes during a working memory task post-ketamine infusion in TRD participants versus healthy volunteers (HVs).
Preprocessing of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) data can be performed in many different ways and often involves manual steps, resulting in reduced comparability across analyses and pipelines.

Voxel-level kinetic modeling in total-body dynamic positron emission tomography (TB-PET) enables precise physiological quantification but complicates parameter uncertainty estimation. While generative consistency models (CMs) can rapidly estimate Bayesian posterior distributions, they are constrained by type of tracers, kinetic models, and protocols.

Linking molecular mechanisms with large-scale brain dynamics remains a fundamental challenge in computational psychiatry. Receptor-informed whole-brain models have provided mechanistic insights into pharmacological interventions, yet they have largely relied on single-receptor topographies that cannot explain the collective response of multiple receptor systems.

Alzheimer’s disease arises from interacting amyloid, tau, and neurodegenerative processes, and is associated with large-scale network dysfunction and reduced brain dynamics complexity. However, it remains unclear whether disease progression alters the causal hierarchical organisation of large-scale brain dynamics.

Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus-a core lexico-semantic region-was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants.

An age-related neurovascular impairment in nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and reciprocal Piezo1-dependent vascular vasoconstriction may precede the accumulation of soluble brain proteins such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and disruption of brain fluid homeostasis in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Preclinical studies suggest that restoring these pathways can enhance neurofluid transport and improve cognitive outcomes.

Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) is a refractory form of major depressive disorder (MDD) for which conventional antidepressant strategies are often insufficient. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in TRD, but its biological mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a high-temporal-resolution, noninvasive window into some of the abnormalities underlying Parkinson's disease (PD), yet reported electrophysiological biomarkers vary widely across studies due to differences in preprocessing, feature extraction, and analytical pipelines.

The functional interaction between the central nervous system and autonomic cardiovascular regulation, commonly referred to as Brain-Heart Interaction (BHI), has gained increasing attention in neurology and psychology through the joint analysis of Electroencephalography (EEG) and Electrocardiography (ECG) signals.

Somatic depression is a distinct subtype of major depressive disorder, with a poorer response to treatment, an elevated risk of suicidal behaviour, and a worse prognosis. Interoception, the sense of internal bodily signals, is related to somatic symptoms.

Self-disturbance is a core feature of schizophrenia (SCZ) and may emerge during the prodromal phase. Temporal imprecision has recently been proposed as a core neural mechanism in schizophrenia, primarily demonstrated in faster EEG frequency ranges.
Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system.

General anesthesia has long been understood as a unitary phenomenon driven by neural suppression — a reduction in cortical activity, entropy, and complexity that renders the brain unable to sustain conscious processing.

Neurosurgical patients carry a high and frequently undertreated burden of psychological suffering, acute and chronic pain, and neurological deficits amenable to recovery. The resurgence of psychedelic research has produced relevant evidence in adjacent fields, but its applicability to neurosurgery has not been systematized.

Ketamine produces rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but these benefits diminish within days. Whether intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) can sustain ketamine response and whether such effects are associated with changes in large-scale brain networks are unclear.

Studies reporting novel therapeutic effects of psychedelic drugs are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these findings could remain uncertain for years. Here, we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to define the robust and replicable effects of the psychedelic drug psilocybin on mouse behavior.

Evidence supporting psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy (PAP) for treating posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, and other historically difficult to treat mental health disorders is growing rapidly. Interest from the public and within the US government to provide access to these treatments has also grown.
Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) abuse has emerged as an increasingly serious public health concern, yet effective interventions for N 2 O dependence remain lacking.

Chronic stress induces strong alteration of hippocampal synaptic plasticity, impairing long-term potentiation and facilitating long-term depression, processes thought to be involved in the pathophysiology of depression. Ketamine, a noncompetitive antagonist of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor, has emerged as a fast-acting antidepressant whose action is believed to involve restoring impaired plasticity, though its sustained effects are elusive.

Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently.
Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG.

The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions.

Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed.

This trial is designed to evaluate efficacy and psychological mechanisms of single-dose psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy (PAP) to treat fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), psychiatric (anxiety, depression) distress and quality-of-life (QOL), in 100 outpatients with early-stage breast cancer.

The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether ingestion of a drug called psilocybin can increase the effectiveness of amblyopia therapy in adults with amblyopia. Psilocybin is a naturally-occurring psychoactive compound found in many species of mushrooms.

This was a randomized, parallel, double-blind clinical trial with healthy volunteers Conditions: Healthy Adult Participants. Interventions: Ayahuasca, Esketamine 0.2 mg/kg. Sponsor: University of Sao Paulo. Planned enrolment: 20. Countries: Brazil. Primary outcomes: Subjective pain; Pain tolerance.

Neuroimaging studies have just begun to explore the acute effects of psychedelics on large-scale brain networks' functional organization. Even less is known about the neural correlates of subacute effects taking place days after the psychedelic experience.

Ayahuasca is a plant tea containing the psychedelic 5-HT2A agonist N,N-dimethyltryptamine and harmala monoamine-oxidase inhibitors. Acute administration leads to neurophysiological modifications in brain regions of the default mode network, purportedly through a glutamatergic mechanism. Post-acutely, ayahuasca potentiates mindfulness capacities in volunteers and induces rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant patients.

Aim: Whether the neural dynamics evoked by high-ventilation breathwork resemble those of classical psychedelic states, and whether they track subjective experience depth. Methods: 64-channel EEG in 25 experienced breathwork practitioners, with resting-state recordings interleaved through a naturalistic high-ventilation breathwork session; experience depth and content also recorded. Results: Breathwork produced broadband cortical desynchronisation, higher signal complexity, reduced alpha power and flattened cortical hierarchy, with these effects correlating with subjective depth at minute resolution. The effects were not explained by music listening or active interoception. Conclusion: The authors argue these are shared neural features of psychedelic-like states regardless of induction method, so breathwork may access psychedelic-like cortical states without drugs.

post: Aim: Whether a single moderate psilocybin dose changes self-concept and self-referential neural processing alongside depressive symptoms in major depressive disorder. Methods: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; N = 37 with major depressive disorder given 0.215 mg/kg psilocybin or placebo with psychological support; depression scales, self-concept scale and fMRI self-referential task. Results: Psilocybin reduced depressive symptoms and increased positive self-concept two weeks after dosing relative to placebo, with self-concept change correlated with lower depression scores. Caudate activation was modulated during externally oriented attention after psilocybin, versus self-referential processing after placebo. Conclusion: The authors conclude self-concept and self-referential processing change concurrently with symptom reduction, and call for replication and refined self-focused therapy protocols.

post: Aim: How the 5-HT2A inverse agonist volinanserin affects behaviour and circuit-level brain activity and connectivity in mice, relevant to schizophrenia. Methods: Behavioural battery in mice covering motor, anxiety-like, compulsive-like, reward and learning domains, with brain activity and functional connectivity measured for drug versus vehicle. Results: Volinanserin selectively reduced locomotor activity, leaving anxiety, compulsive-like behaviour, reward and learning unaffected. It raised activity in the lateral septum, dorsal raphe and nucleus accumbens, lowered prefrontal activity, and reduced lateral septum connectivity with prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and amygdala. Conclusion: The authors conclude the lateral septum is a key locus for volinanserin's putative antipsychotic effects, supporting its role in 5-HT2A-targeting drug action.

post: Aim: Whether a DMT and harmine meditation retreat changes the brain's control energy landscape in the subacute afterglow window. Methods: Exploratory analysis of rs-fMRI from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 39) before and after a three-day retreat, with control energy computed on a group structural connectome under two timescale approaches. Results: No global shift in control energy between transitions, though mean control energy rose in both groups under the long-timescale approach. The central executive network showed a post-retreat increase in the verum group surviving FDR correction, and the visual network decreased under the short-timescale approach. Conclusion: The authors conclude effects are network- and timescale-specific rather than global, but small, heterogeneous and needing confirmation in larger samples.

post: Aim: Whether LSD quantification across Swiss drug checking laboratories is accurate and reproducible. Methods: Interlaboratory ring trial across five Swiss drug checking services using HPLC-DAD, GC-MS and HPLC-MS/MS on two LSD-infused blotters and one methanolic solution, with results corrected by qNMR-determined purity. Results: Relative standard deviations were 8%–16.5% and mean accuracy −5.3% to −13.0%, with more variability for the liquid sample and the largest deviations from mass spectrometry methods. Conclusion: The authors conclude current LSD quantification is reliable in drug checking settings and provide a basis for future proficiency testing, noting stability and production factors as possible sources of discrepancy.

post: Aim: What mechanisms underlie the rapid and lasting antidepressant effects of ketamine and classical psychedelics, centred on synaptic and circuit plasticity. Methods: Narrative review, based on a 2026 Society for Neuroscience minisymposium, covering hippocampal, prefrontal and accumbal mechanisms for ketamine and comparing these with psilocybin. Results: Review of BDNF/TrkB, mGluR5, ERK-DUSP6 and GPCR-dependent plasticity mechanisms across regions and cell types for ketamine, with psilocybin's 5-HT2A-mediated effects compared. Conclusion: The authors argue antidepressant efficacy arises from coordinated, temporally staged plasticity across molecules, synapses, cells and circuits rather than a single pathway.

post: Aim: What candidate substrates could sustain the persistent effects of a single psychedelic dose across the days-to-weeks consolidation window. Methods: Narrative review of intracellular 5-HT2A pools, neurotrophin convergence and cortical H3K27ac epigenomic data, with evidence graded as established, indirect or hypothetical and six falsifiable criteria proposed. Results: Cited data show persistent bidirectional H3K27ac changes at seven days in mouse frontal cortex after one compound, interpreted as a displaced regulatory set-point rather than a retained mark. Conclusion: The authors conclude the evidence is narrow and that claims of persistence over weeks concern behaviour rather than chromatin state, offering falsifiable tests.

post: Aim: Whether the fluorine-18 PET radiotracer [18F]GPR39 2.1 can specifically image the zinc-sensing receptor GPR39 in vivo. Methods: Preclinical study in cell uptake assays, rats with pharmacological blockade, GPR39 knockout mice, 5xFAD transgenic mice, PET imaging, biodistribution and autoradiography. Results: Brain uptake fell by up to about 90% under blockade in rats, by 76% by PET and 90% by biodistribution in knockout mice, and was reduced in 5xFAD mice, with good stability and brain penetration. Conclusion: The authors conclude [18F]GPR39 2.1 is a stable, brain-penetrant and highly specific tracer for noninvasive GPR39 imaging, supporting its use as an imaging and therapeutic target.

post: Aim: Whether data-driven factors from clinical EEG differ across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative dementia phenotypes. Methods: 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET within one year; six EEG factors from nonnegative tensor decomposition compared across 14 StateViewer diagnostic classes, adjusted for a slowing index and related to regional metabolism and cognition (n = 98). Results: Four oscillatory factors varied across phenotypes, most strongly in dementia with Lewy bodies, dysexecutive Alzheimer disease and posterior cortical atrophy. Slowing explained much of the alpha and beta effects, while posterior theta-slow alpha stayed phenotype-specific after adjustment. Conclusion: The authors conclude decomposed clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artefact in ways tracking metabolic phenotype, supporting scalable EEG-based dementia phenotyping, though frontotemporal phenotypes were poorly discriminated.

post: Aim: Whether individualised theta-frequency tACS over the prefrontal cortex is feasible and tolerable in moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder, and what clinical and EEG changes accompany it. Methods: Open-label pilot of 11 adults with MDD receiving 20 sessions of bilateral prefrontal theta tACS (1.5 mA peak-to-peak, 20 min) during working memory tasks, with frequency individualised from task EEG; 10 completed treatment. Results: MADRS scores fell significantly from baseline to midpoint, endpoint and follow-up. Response rates were 80% and remission 60% at endpoint, rising to 80% and 70% at follow-up. Greater ITF power increases tracked larger MADRS reductions, though group-level power changes were not significant. Conclusion: The authors conclude that the approach is feasible and provides preliminary observations to inform sham-controlled trials, cautioning that the open-label design and small sample limit interpretation and allow placebo effects.

post: Aim: Whether multishell diffusion MRI models can detect ketamine-induced dendritic and synaptic microstructural changes in mouse brain in vivo. Methods: In vivo multishell dMRI with diffusion tensor, NODDI and diffusion kurtosis models in wild-type and SAPAP3 knockout mice after ketamine, with histology for synapse markers and Monte Carlo simulations of dendritic diffusion. Results: Histology confirmed ketamine-induced increases in cortical synapse markers, but dMRI metrics did not change. Simulations showed sensitivity to small morphological changes only in noiseless conditions, whereas the acquisitions detected baseline differences between sexes and genotypes. Conclusion: The authors conclude that the dMRI acquisition and modelling approaches used lack sensitivity to the subtle dendritic changes induced by ketamine.

post: Aim: Whether repeated administration of the cannabinoid agonist nabilone changes brain FAAH availability measured with [11C]CURB PET. Methods: Exploratory Phase IV pilot with ten healthy adults, each scanned at baseline and after a 7-day nabilone regimen titrated to 2 mg/day; FAAH quantified with a two-tissue irreversible model and analysed with repeated-measures ANCOVA including genotype. Results: Nabilone increased marijuana-like effects (p = 0.004) and reduced energy (p = 0.02) and clear-headedness (p = 0.01). No detectable mean change in FAAH across brain regions was observed (p = 0.357). Conclusion: The authors conclude that no detectable change in brain FAAH followed seven days of nabilone, a preliminary finding needing confirmation in larger controlled studies.

post: Aim: Whether stress-induced dopamine release in the striatum relates to changes in striatal-prefrontal functional connectivity in nicotine-dependent individuals. post: Aim: Quantify how sample size affects the reliability of EEG case-control findings across psychiatric conditions in children and adolescents. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 2,874 participants aged 5–18 years, including ADHD, autism, anxiety, learning disorders and controls, with spectral, temporal and complexity features compared across repeated random subsamples of varying size. Results: Small samples gave unstable, inflated and highly variable effect sizes, while larger samples converged on consistent but small effects. post: Aim: Whether cannabis use alters large-scale brain organisation, tested as changes in low-frequency connectome harmonics using 7T resting-state fMRI. Methods: Human Connectome Project 7T data from 81 cannabis users and 81 matched non-users; BOLD activity projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; t-tests with FDR correction and atlas localisation. Results: Cannabis users showed significantly greater power in one low-frequency harmonic (k = 6; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; d = 0.659), roughly 44% higher than non-users, localised to a frontoparietal–sensorimotor network. post: Aim: Whether physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density in corticolimbic regions of the living human brain. Methods: PET with [18F]SynVesT-1 in 51 individuals (61% female), grouped as physically active or insufficiently active; group comparisons, regression and mediation analyses including BMI and depressive symptoms. Conclusion: Physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density, particularly in prefrontal circuits, partly independent of BMI. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality.

post: Aim: Whether bergenin, an anti-inflammatory isocoumarin, reverses anxiety- and depression-like behaviour induced by antibiotic-driven gut dysbiosis in mice. Methods: Antibiotic regimen in Swiss albino mice followed by 14 days of bergenin (25 or 50 mg/kg/day) or fluoxetine; elevated plus maze, open field, forced swim and tail suspension tests; docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics against TLR4-MD-2 and SERT. Results: Bergenin dose-dependently attenuated anxiety- and depression-like deficits, with high-dose recovery of about 70-92%, without altering behaviour in antibiotic-free animals. In silico, it bound the SERT S1 site with stability resembling fluoxetine, but its TLR4-MD-2 interaction was shallow. Conclusion: Bergenin ameliorates behavioural deficits in antibiotic-treated mice, and in silico data favour serotonergic over TLR4 involvement. The authors stress that the work is hypothesis-generating and that microbiome and mechanistic assays were not performed.

post: Aim: Whether EEG biomarkers for major depressive disorder that are stable across data subsets generalise better than those with the strongest predictive signal. Methods: EEG from 30 MDD patients and 88 controls; connectivity, spectral and complexity features; XGBoost pipeline with leakage-free cross-validation and a nested Stability-Optimized Consensus Learning framework. Results: Theta and alpha features gave the strongest signal (max AUC 0.683) but were unstable across subsets (mean Jaccard 0.187) and overfitted. A model built on stable consensus biomarkers generalised better (AUC 0.792 vs 0.662) with less overfitting (P < .05). Conclusion: The MDD signature exists as a potent but unstable theta-alpha signal and a weaker but stable connectome signal. The authors argue stability matters more than strength for clinical biomarkers.

post: Aim: Whether individualised functional connectivity-guided iTBS targeting left DLPFC improves depression and anhedonia in adolescents who have not responded to antidepressants. post: Aim: How local near-criticality within brain regions interacts with global criticality when regions are coupled through a mouse connectome. Methods: Multiscale model with neural mass models tuned near the asynchronous-synchronous transition, coupled via an empirical mouse connectome, plus whole-brain simulations of connectome-coupled spiking neurons. post: Aim: Whether cardiac phase modulates periodic and aperiodic MEG activity differently in major depressive disorder. Methods: Simultaneous resting MEG and ECG in 60 patients and 60 matched controls, with a 6-month follow-up; SPRiNT separation of periodic and aperiodic activity; linear mixed models and permutation statistics. post: Aim: To audit how rodent psychedelic studies are designed and whether their conditions and assays could translate to human therapy. Methods: Systematic review of 266 rodent psychedelic studies published 2014 to 2026, assessing welfare and set-and-setting-like factors, behavioural assay design, and individual and social factors. Results: Most studies included stress-inducing factors: only 14% tested in the active phase, 7% used environmental enrichment, and 21% used refined handling. Drug administration almost universally used restraint-requiring methods. Most assays were brief and isolated, and group-level cross-sectional designs dominated. Conclusion: The authors argue translation requires longitudinal tracking of individuals in enriched social settings with comprehensive behavioural characterisation.

Software framework combining a constrained local language model, literature retrieval, provenance tracking and cross-platform tests, applied to public EEG and MEG datasets.
Results

Action-selection accuracy was 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG. 142 cross-platform tests showed close numerical agreement. Spectral, network, decoding and source analyses were demonstrated on public data.
Conclusion
The toolbox offers a researcher-controlled, reproducible environment running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs.
why_you: Relevant to your EEG and MEG analysis workflows and reproducibility, and could reduce friction in your neurodynamics pipelines.

post: Aim: To update the Human Neocortical Neurosolver canonical circuit model with electrophysiology and dendritic dynamics tuned to human tissue. Methods: Biophysical multiscale model of L2/3 and L5 pyramidal and interneuron circuits, tuned to human recordings, with simulations of event-related responses and oscillations linked to E/MEG signals. Results: The updated model reproduces realistic somatic dynamics, simulates dendritic calcium spikes in L5 ET neurons and shorter dendritic spikes in L2/3 pyramidal cells, and separates somatic, synaptic and dendritic contributions to E/MEG. Conclusion: The model enables validation against in vitro and in vivo data and gives mechanistic insight into E/MEG signatures.

post: Aim: To identify the molecular signal that draws cannibalistic locusts to injured conspecifics. Methods: Behavioural assays, olfactory receptor knockdowns, and bacterial gene-cluster deletions in Locusta migratoria, examining the symbiont-derived volatile guaiacol. Results: Guaiacol, released more after injury, attracts nymphs and triggers cannibalism via receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34. It is made by the symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei; deleting its gene cluster abolished production and behavioural effects. At low levels it activates immune pathways. Conclusion: A microbial-chemical signal links immune defence with cannibalism, offering molecular targets for population manipulation.

post: Aim: To determine how nuclear RNA quality control decides the fate of poised intron-containing polyadenylated pre-mRNAs. Methods: Molecular and genetic study in mouse and human cells, including NCBP3 depletion and pathogenic RNA exosome mutations, with analysis of mitochondrial function and motor behaviour. Results: NCBP3 favours splicing of poised pre-mRNAs while anillin favours exosome degradation; many affected transcripts encode mitochondrial factors. NCBP3 loss or exosome mutations reduced mitochondrial activity, causing muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination and poorer motor coordination. Conclusion: A competition between pre-mRNA pathways controls mitochondrial function, and its disruption contributes to neurological disease.

post: Aim: To test whether later-born generations enter old age with better memory and decline more slowly, and whether this explains falling dementia incidence. Methods: Analysis of about 783,000 episodic-memory assessments from about 219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed up to 30 years, including hippocampal volumes. Results: Later-born generations showed higher memory levels in old age and slower subsequent decline, a double advantage large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade fall in dementia incidence. Slower decline was mirrored by lower clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Conclusion: Sustaining the dementia decline requires prevention that protects brain health across the lifespan, starting in childhood.

post: Aim: To test whether a single psilocybin dose changes synaptic density (SV2A) and 5-HT2A receptor density in the pig brain. Methods: Twenty-four awake pigs received psilocybin 0.08 mg/kg or saline intravenously and were euthanised at one or seven days. Autoradiography of hippocampus and prefrontal cortex used [3H]UCB-J, [3H]MDL100907 and [3H]Cimbi-36. Results: One day after psilocybin, hippocampal SV2A density was 4.42% higher and 5-HT2A density was lower in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex (−15.21% to −50.19%), significant for hippocampus across ligands and for prefrontal cortex with Cimbi-36 only. At seven days SV2A remained higher (+9.24% hippocampus, +6.10% prefrontal cortex), with no 5-HT2A differences. Conclusion: Psilocybin may cause persistent synaptogenesis and an acute fall in 5-HT2A density, possibly contributing to antidepressant effects.

post: Aim: To characterise how the spatiotemporal complexity of EEG activity changes across subanesthetic and anaesthetic doses of ketamine. Methods: High-density scalp EEG in healthy volunteers during subanesthetic and anaesthetic ketamine. Hidden Markov modelling classified brain states, and Lempel-Ziv complexity was computed per state after controlling for spectral changes. Results: Subanesthetic ketamine raised complexity relative to baseline. Anaesthetic ketamine produced alternating low and high complexity before stabilising at a high level comparable to baseline. Conclusion: Ketamine-induced state transitions share features of anaesthesia, normal consciousness and altered consciousness, illustrating its complex pharmacological properties.

post: Aim: To review preclinical and human evidence on how classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) alter sleep architecture, sleep quality, EEG activity and dreams. Methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed up to May 2026; twelve eligible preclinical and clinical studies, with validity assessed by appropriate quality tools. Results: Preclinical studies consistently showed acute REM suppression, delayed REM onset and increased wakefulness. Human findings were heterogeneous: psilocybin prolonged REM latency, ayahuasca reduced REM duration, and slow-wave activity results were mixed. Conclusion: Classic psychedelics cause acute but transient sleep changes, mainly in REM sleep. Whether these contribute to therapeutic effects is uncertain, and the review was not prospectively registered.

post: Aim: To test whether simulated low-count [18F]FDG PET/MR preserves diagnostic quality and epileptogenic zone lateralisation in paediatric epilepsy. Methods: Twenty-seven paediatric patients with epilepsy; list-mode data truncated to simulate 50%, 65% and 80% count reductions, analysed with ROI- and voxel-based lateralisation methods. Results: Contrast-to-noise fell and coefficient of variation rose with count reduction. Image quality stayed clinically acceptable up to 65% reduction, with consistent SUVRs and unchanged lateralisation agreement with the clinical consensus. Conclusion: A 65% simulated count reduction preserved acceptable image quality and lateralisation in paediatric epilepsy, supporting future lower-activity validation studies.

post: Aim: To characterise spectral and entropy-based EEG signatures of each jhana state of advanced concentration absorption meditation and relate them to experience. Methods: High-density EEG in 20 advanced meditators across eight ACAM-J states, with a multidimensional battery of spectral and complexity measures and phenomenological ratings. Results: Widespread posterior-central reductions in oscillatory and aperiodic power, posterior aperiodic flattening, and rising entropy-based complexity. Complexity stayed elevated in the most minimal states, and between practitioners higher entropy accompanied visual and auditory content. Conclusion: ACAM-J is a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of altered consciousness, revealing a dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness.

post: Aim: To compare intensity normalisation methods for [18F]FDG PET in dementia with Lewy bodies, identifying the most suitable approach. Methods: [18F]FDG PET/MR in 110 DLB patients and 30 controls; reference-region, proportional scaling, iterative and histogram-based methods compared on normative alignment, disease independence, stability and simulated phantom recovery. Results: Reference-region normalisation gave smaller DLB-control scaling differences, weaker meta-ROI correlations and lower variability than data-driven methods. The white matter and pons had the highest composite scores. Conclusion: Reference-region normalisation is preferred in DLB, outperforming proportional scaling, histogram and data-driven approaches in this large cohort.
